what: H&R Block prepares tax returns. It operates thousands of offices in the United States where people have their taxes done by an assistant, sells software for those who prefer to do it themselves, and offers related financial products including refund advances and a prepaid banking account.
customers: American individual taxpayers, particularly those with complicated circumstances or who simply do not want to do it themselves, plus small businesses needing bookkeeping and tax help.
money: Returns prepared in offices by trained tax professionals.
Software and online tax preparation for self-filers.
Refund transfers, advances, the Spruce banking product and small business services.
moat: Tax preparation is bought on trust, which favours a name people recognise, and the compressed season means physical offices and trained staff in place by February are a real barrier. Customers also return year after year because the previous year’s return is already on file, which makes the next one quicker and cheaper to produce.
risks: The long-term threat is that tax filing becomes free and automatic, whether through government programmes or improved software, which would remove the reason to pay anyone.
Revenue is heavily concentrated in a few months, so a disrupted filing season has no opportunity to be made up.
Revenue growth is slow, from $3.5B in 2022 to $3.9B in 2026, which is barely ahead of price increases.
Debt of $2.1B against $958.7M of cash is material for a business with modest growth.
Only three analysts cover the stock, so the $53.00 average target rests on minimal coverage.
opportunities: The shares trade at about 8.4 times earnings, 7.7 times EV/EBITDA and 7.6 times free cash flow — a very low price.
Free cash flow of $746.9M against a $5.6B market value is a 13% yield, which has funded large buybacks.
A net margin of 18.6% is strong, because the cost base is seasonal staff rather than permanent infrastructure.
Customers return annually and their prior return is on file, which makes repeat business cheap to serve.
Many taxpayers want a person to be responsible for their return, and that preference has proven durable through every wave of software.
watch: The number of returns prepared and revenue per return. The business grows by charging more rather than serving more people, and the volume figure tells you whether the customer base is eroding.
view: H&R Block is one of the cheapest cash-generative businesses in the American market, and the discount has a specific cause worth stating plainly: a meaningful number of people believe tax preparation is eventually going away. Free government filing, better software, and in time automated returns all point in the same direction, and if filing becomes genuinely free and automatic, there is no reason to pay anyone to do it. That is the bear case and it is not silly.

What the bear case has consistently underestimated is how durable the preference for a person is. Software has been able to prepare a simple return for thirty years, and millions of people still drive to an office in February and pay someone to do it. They are buying responsibility rather than arithmetic — someone to blame, someone to sign, someone to call if a letter arrives. That is not a technology problem, and it has survived every wave of software so far.

The economics are excellent and get little credit. An 18.6% net margin, $747 million of free cash flow on $4 billion of revenue, and a cost base that is largely seasonal — offices and trained staff ramping up for a few months rather than permanent infrastructure. The shares trade at about 7.6 times free cash flow, a 13% yield, and management has been using it to buy back a great deal of stock. Against flat revenue, a shrinking share count is how the per-share figures grow.

So the honest framing is that you are being paid a 13% cash yield to take the obsolescence risk, and that the risk is real but slow. Revenue growth of $3.5 billion to $3.9 billion over five years tells you the business is not growing so much as holding and raising prices. Returns prepared is the number that reveals which way this is going — if volume is eroding while revenue holds on price increases, the end comes eventually, and the buyback is simply the most efficient way to harvest a declining asset. That is still a perfectly good investment at this multiple; it is just worth knowing which one you own.
bull: The preference for a person handling your return proves durable, price increases offset flat volumes, and a 13% free cash flow yield shrinks the share count aggressively.
bear: Free and automated filing finally takes hold, returns prepared decline faster than prices rise, and a leveraged business harvests itself to nothing.
